KEY MESSAGE 1...Latest surface analysis shows a large and 
strengthening low pressure system currently around 300 miles due
east of Cape Hatteras as of this mornings update with showers 
wrapping around this low, mainly across the offshore waters. 
Overall, very little change in forecast thinking as a mid level
shortwave is forecast to round the base of an upper level 
trough currently located along the Eastern Seaboard this morning.
This mid level shortwave will act to rapidly deepen the 
aforementioned surface low as it slowly shifts north in the 
coming days, bringing a prolonged period of gusty N/NE winds and
dangerous coastal and marine conditions to ENC. 

There continues to be further clarity with this Nor'Easter's 
eventual track with much of the guidance slowly coming into 
agreement with the ECMWF solution of a slightly slower N'ward 
track and strong low stalling just south of Long Island this 
weekend. As a result, stronger winds are forecast to linger 
along the coast, especially north of Hatteras prolonging some 
coastal impacts. Regarding sensible weather, isolated showers 
may continue along the OBX today into tonight but otherwise the 
biggest concerns over the next 24 hours will be the ongoing wind
and coastal impacts. 

By far, the greatest impacts with this Nor'easter remain across
the Outer Banks. Here, continued moderate to strong northeast 
to north winds remain in place, and potentially last into 
Saturday morning. Wind Advisories have ended across mainland
Dare County, Ocracoke, and East Carteret, but remain in effect 
across the OBX from Hatteras Island north into this evening as 
gusts up to 45-50 mph won't be out of the question today as the
Nor'Easter slowly pulls away from ENC. This may lead to some 
minor tree and power line damage, along with a risk of isolated 
power outages. Roads along the Outer Banks may be dangerous to 
traverse for high profile vehicles, especially along bridges. 
NC-12 from the Basnight Bridge to Rodanthe remains closed due to
ocean overwash. 

The strong, and long duration, of the winds is also expected to
support an increased risk of coastal impacts. Seas are already
dangerous, reaching heights of about 13-19 ft at 13-14 seconds 
north of Cape Hatteras and 8-12 ft south. Seas have likely
peaked this morning, but dangerous surf conditions in addition 
to a risk of beach erosion, wave runup, ocean overwash, and 
minor to moderate coastal flooding will continue into tonight as
seas will be slow to lower. This will likely result in impacts 
to vulnerable portions of the Outer Banks north of Ocracoke 
Inlet where dune structures are compromised or non- existent. At
this point the 6-8ft+ wave heights in the surf zone may last 
into this weekend. A High Surf Advisory Remains in effect 
through Saturday evening.

For soundside areas adjacent to the southern Pamlico Sound, and
the nearby Neuse River, persistent north to northeasterly winds
will continue to lead to minor coastal flooding into this 
morning before water levels begin to gradually recede. Some 
gauges in the southern Pamlico Sound have already approached or
have reached minor flood levels and continue to do so this
morning. With winds becoming more northerly this morning, this 
is forecast to allow the soundside coastal flooding risk to 
shift to portions of Ocracoke and Hatteras Villages.

Please continue to stay tuned for future updates as this is a
complex and longer-duration Nor'easter, with subtle changes in 
strength and path of the low leading to increased, or decreased,
coastal impacts.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
As the low shifts to New England and eventually weakens, sfc 
high and ridging aloft builds into ENC early next week. This 
will bring lighter winds, sunshine, and warmer weather back to 
the region. Of note, despite the warming weather, dewpoints are
forecast to remain in the 50s into midweek next week, making 
for more comfortable conditions despite highs warming up into 
the mid to upper 80s. Slightly higher dewpoints into the 60s
look to return closer to the end of next week.
